statechart_spawn(Pid, [
       src_text('<!--

    Pause and resume: hierarchy and history states.

    A compound state can remember which of its substates was active when
    it was last exited, and return there later. The `play` region cycles
    between s1 and s2 on the `play` and `reset` events. A `pause` event
    leaves that region for `interrupted`; `resume` goes to the history
    state `h`, which restores whichever of s1 or s2 was active when the
    pause happened, instead of starting over at s1. The `stop` event runs
    the whole machine to its final state. Watch the trace to see the
    remembered substate come back on resume.

    Run the chart and send it events from the Queries menu.
    Keep the Logger open and SXML trace selected.

-->

<statechart version="0.2" initial="game">
    <state id="game" initial="play">
        <state id="play" initial="s1">
            <history id="h">
                <go to="s1" />
            </history>
            <state id="s1">
                <go to="s2" on="play" />
            </state>
            <state id="s2">
                <go to="s1" on="reset" />
            </state>
            <go to="interrupted" on="pause" />
        </state>
        <state id="interrupted">
            <go to="h" on="resume" />
        </state>
        <go to="final" on="stop" />
    </state>
    <final id="final" />
</statechart>

       src_text('<!--

    Deferred events: postponing what a state cannot yet handle.

    A state can mark certain events to be kept for later rather than
    dropped. In the initialising state, command/1 events match <defer>,
    so any that arrive are held in arrival order instead of being
    discarded. The initialised event then moves the chart to the ready
    state, where the deferred commands are re-offered, and handled,
    before any newer external event is accepted. Send two command/1
    events first, then initialised, and watch the held commands run in
    the order they came in.

    Run the chart and send it events from the Queries menu.
    Keep the Logger open and SXML trace selected.

    <state id="initialising">
        <onentry>
            writeln(''Initialising...'')
        </onentry>
        <defer on="command(_)"/>
        <go to="ready" on="initialised"/>
    </state>

    <state id="ready">
        <onentry>
            writeln(''Ready.'')
        </onentry>
        <go on="command(Command)">

statechart_spawn(Pid, [
       src_text('<!--

    Transitive closure with eventless transitions.

    A chart can compute, not only react. The <datamodel> seeds the Prolog
    facts p(a,b), p(b,c), p(c,d). The single working state has an
    eventless transition whose guard looks for a missing link (p(X,Y) and
    p(Y,Z) but not yet p(X,Z)) and whose body asserts it. Needing no
    event, the chart keeps taking that transition, adding one new edge
    each time, until the guard can no longer be satisfied. A second
    guarded transition then collects the finished relation and moves to
    the final state. It demonstrates eventless (automatic) transitions,
    guards that run real Prolog queries, and the chart''s own logical
    database used as working memory.

    Run the chart from the Queries menu.
    Keep the Logger open and SXML trace selected.
    
-->

<statechart version="0.2" initial="s">
    <datamodel>
        p(a,b). 
        p(b,c). 
        p(c,d).
    </datamodel>
    <state id="s">
        <go if="p(X,Y), p(Y,Z), \\+p(X,Z)">
            assert(p(X,Z))
        </go>
        <go to="f" if="findall(p(X,Y), p(X,Y), List)">
            format("Closure: ~w", [List])
        </go>
    </state>
    <final id="f"/>
</statechart>

statechart_spawn(Pid, [
       src_text('<!--

    Greatest common divisor by Euclid''s subtractive algorithm.

    A computation expressed as a statechart. The <datamodel> declares a
    dynamic int/1 relation; the event integers(List) seeds it with a set
    of numbers. In the `run` state, an eventless transition repeatedly
    finds two stored numbers where one is larger and replaces the larger
    by their difference. When no such pair remains, a single value is
    left: the GCD of the whole set, which the last transition prints.
    Like the closure example, it drives itself forward with guarded
    eventless transitions over the Prolog database.

    Run the chart and send it events from the Queries menu.
    Keep the Logger open and SXML trace selected.

-->

<statechart version="0.2" initial="init">
    <datamodel>
        :- dynamic int/1.
    </datamodel>
    <state id="init">
        <go on="integers(List)" to="run">
            forall(member(X, List), asserta(int(X)))
        </go>
    </state>
    <state id="run">
        <go if="int(X), int(Y), X > Y">
            Z is X-Y,
            retract(int(X)),
            assert(int(Z))
        </go>
        <go to="stop" if="int(X)">
            writeln(X)
        </go>
    </state>
    <final id="stop" />
</statechart>

statechart_spawn(Pid, [
       src_text('<!--

    Shared database: reaching node knowledge from a chart.

    A statechart''s executable content runs in an actor whose logical
    environment includes the node''s shared database, so a chart can build
    on knowledge it did not define itself. Here summary/2 and
    local_label/1 are local to the chart, but summary/2 also calls
    shared_fact/1, which lives in the node database, and local_label/1
    shadows a predicate of the same name there, so the local clause wins.
    An eventless guard likewise consults the shared predicate
    shared_transition_enabled/0 to decide when to move on. It shows how
    local and shared knowledge combine, and how a local definition takes
    precedence over a shared one.

    Run the chart from the Queries menu.
    Keep the Logger open and SXML trace selected.

-->

<statechart version="0.2" initial="start">
    <datamodel> 
        local_label(statechart_datamodel).
        
        summary(Node, Local) :-
            shared_fact(Node),
            local_label(Local).
    </datamodel>

    <state id="start">
        <onentry>
            summary(Node, Local),
            output(result(Node, Local))
        </onentry>
        <go if="shared_transition_enabled" to="done" />
    </state>

    <final id="done">
        <onentry>output(''DONE'')</onentry>

</statechart>

    run a DCG, a history state for retrying, and onentry actions that

        adj(color(blue)) --> [blue].
        adj(size(small)) --> [small].

statechart_spawn(Pid, [
       src_text('<!--

    Spawning a plain actor from a statechart.

    The <spawn> element lets a statechart create and oversee an ordinary
    Web Prolog actor. Here the chart spawns a `ponger` actor, whose code
    is given inline, and learns its pid through the spawned(Pid) event. It
    registers that pid under the name `ponger` and then plays ping-pong
    with it: the Pinger state sends ping and, on each pong reply, waits
    and sends another. It bridges the two worlds of this demonstrator, a
    statechart on one side and a bare receive-loop actor on the other,
    talking by message.

    Run the chart from the Queries menu.
    Keep the Logger open and SXML trace selected.

-->

<statechart version="0.2" initial="Pingpong">
    <state id="Pingpong" initial="Init">
        <spawn type="actor" goal="ponger" options="[monitor(true)]">
            ponger :-
                receive({
                    ping(Pid) ->
                        sleep(1),
                        Pid ! pong,
                        ponger
                 }).
        </spawn>
        <state id="Init">
            <go to="Pinger" on="spawned(Pid)">
                register(ponger, Pid)
            </go>
        </state>
        <state id="Pinger">
            <onentry>
                self(Self),
                ponger ! ping(Self)
            </onentry>
            <go on="pong">
                writeln(''Received Pong''),
                sleep(1),
                self(Self),
                ponger ! ping(Self)
            </go>
        </state>
    </state>
</statechart>

    finishes. It is the statechart-level view of getting answers one at a
    time from a running goal.

    Run the chart from the Queries menu.
    Keep the Logger open and SXML trace selected.

-->

<statechart version="0.2" initial="spawn-ask-collect">
    <state id="spawn-ask-collect" initial="ask">
        <spawn type="toplevel" options="[time_limit(30)]">
            q(X) :- p(X).
            p(a). p(b). p(c). p(d).
        </spawn>
        <state id="ask">
            <go to="collect" on="spawned(Pid)">
                toplevel_call(Pid, q(X), [
                    limit(1)
                ])
            </go>
        </state>
        <state id="collect">
            <go to="collect" on="success(Pid, Data, true)">
                writeln(Data),
                toplevel_next(Pid)
            </go>
            <go to="final" on="success(_, Data, false)">
                writeln(Data)
            </go>
        </state>
    </state>
    <final id="final" />
</statechart>
